fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. The disciples ask a big question and Jesus doesn't give them a speech first. He invites a little child to stand among them (Matthew 18:2). Sometimes the best answer is just a little one standing right there among them.
No mountain trip here, friend. The text says Jesus invited a little child to stand among them (Matthew 18:2). Nobody had to hike anywhere for this lesson.

That's a different moment, baker. In John 8:6, Jesus writes on the ground with His finger. Here, He doesn't write anything. He invites a little child to stand among the disciples (Matthew 18:2). The whole lesson is standing right there on two small feet.

I get why that sounds right, baker. But Jesus doesn't mention a reward here. He says unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 18:3). The change He names is becoming like little children.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 18:4). The disciples asked who ranks highest, and Jesus invited a little child to stand among them. I'm still waiting on a trophy for MY humility, which tells you how I'm doing.

Nice try, baker. Jesus doesn't give the title to the longest follower. He says whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 18:4). Time on the counter doesn't count here.

Good instinct to look twice, friend, but this one is true. Jesus says, "And whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me." (Matthew 18:5). Read the end again: "welcomes Me." Jesus says it Himself, and I had to read it twice too.
Not quite, friend. The verse names someone else. Jesus says, "…woe to the man through whom they come!" (Matthew 18:7). The answer this card wants is the man through whom the stumbling blocks come.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father in heaven." (Matthew 18:10). That's the reason He gives for not looking down on any of these little ones. I think it's worth a slow read.

Good thought, friend, but that's not the reason Jesus gives here. His reason is that their angels in heaven always see the face of His Father in heaven (Matthew 18:10). Inheriting the earth isn't mentioned in this passage.

That's right, baker. Jesus asks, "…will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost?" (Matthew 18:12). One sheep out of a hundred has gone astray, and the man goes out to search for it.

Good guess, baker, but no servants show up. Jesus says the man will "…go out to search for the one that is lost?" (Matthew 18:12). No delegating, no "can somebody go check on that sheep?" Just the man, going out to search.
Right, friend. Jesus says, "…he rejoices more over that one sheep than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray." (Matthew 18:13). Look at that word, "more." That's the whole answer.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, "If he listens to you, you have won your brother over." (Matthew 18:15). Notice what you win: your brother. Getting him back is the prize.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "…if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven." (Matthew 18:19). When two of you on the earth agree about what you ask for, it is the Father who does it.
No prophet in this verse, baker. Jesus says, "For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them." (Matthew 18:20). The only one He names as being there is Himself.
